rv.q: In the meantime, this medicinal froth gives the West End a perfect shot in the arm.
Even if you don’t consider the pratfall to be the high watermark of human achievement, you’ll find the sheer chutzpah here pretty irresistible.
The physical comedy is enjoyably frenetic, and there's a potent chemistry between the leads.
While I laughed freely and often, there’s nothing subtle about this short production.
But the fight scenes — the slapstick violence essential to any farce — are feeble.
The proceedings are enjoyable but rarely generate the requisite helpless hilarity and have a rather dated feel.
But the plot is without tension. No one is in danger of losing their reputation – along with their trousers or their mind – so nothing matters.
But The Painkiller is too much flab and fluff and flannel, with nowhere near enough sharp edges.
Branagh is a great actor who knows how to act farce, mostly through underplaying, and he's very funny...
How good a time you'll have at this latest offering, THE PAINKILLER, will depend on your sense of humour.
I laughed outright on a couple of occasions and winced pretty much throughout.
And it is one of the funniest plays on the West End stage at the moment.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this French farce revival, with some finding Branagh and Brydon's physical comedy "hilarious" and "frenetic," while others deem it "dated," "excruciating," or "thunderously unfunny."
